Yes—very likely.

The Moon is **37° above the horizon**, toward azimuth **217°** (southwest), while the Sun is already **13.5° below the horizon**. With only **26% illumination**, it will be a crescent, but it should still be conspicuous in a clear sky. Its angular separation from the Sun is **61°**, so it is well clear of the Sun’s glare and is not an especially challenging twilight observation.

Look roughly **southwest, about halfway up the sky**. In Cairo at that time, the main practical issue would be finding the correct part of the sky—not the Moon’s faintness. It should be visible to normal unaided eyesight, assuming no buildings, haze, dust, or bright local lighting obscure it.
